tldr: The authors propose a framework that bridges the skeletal and finger-length morphology gaps between human and robot hands through optimization, faithfully reproduces contact relationships, and learns zero-shot real-world visuomotor policies directly from human hand motion data.
hero_caption: The three stages of Morphometric Optimization (MMO), the core of the proposed method. The morphology of the MANO model itself is optimized to match the target robot hand skeleton, contact relationships are restored, and dense skeleton blending with inverse kinematics converts the motion into robot joint commands.
overview:
Human hand-object interaction (HOI) data is an attractive source of demonstrations for achieving dexterous robot manipulation. However, transferring flexible human hand motions and contacts to robot hands is not easy. Robots and human hands have vastly different structures (morphologies), including finger counts and link lengths. Moreover, simply transferring hand trajectories kinematically causes hands to slip or bounce in physics simulation, dropping the objects.

"Morphometric Imitation," proposed in this paper, elegantly solves this challenge through a three-stage pipeline. In the first stage, "Morphometric Optimization (MMO)," the finger lengths and palm of the human hand model (MANO) are deformed and optimized to match the robot, and contact relationships disrupted by deformation are restored frame by frame. In the second stage, taking this contact-preserving kinematic trajectory as an initial reference, residual reinforcement learning (Residual RL) jointly achieves object pose tracking and finger contact matching to produce dynamically feasible, stable demonstration trajectories. In the third stage, these demonstrations are distilled into a point-cloud-based visuomotor policy.

Evaluated across three robot hands (3-finger, 4-finger, and 5-finger) and ten manipulation tasks, MMO improved the contact F1 score by more than 8 points over existing kinematic retargeting baselines. Furthermore, it boosted the success rate of subsequent residual RL by up to 35 points. The resulting visuomotor policies were deployed directly onto a real 7-DoF arm with a 5-finger hand, achieving an 89.3% zero-shot success rate across 300 real-world trials on 30 objects.
contributions: Developed MMO, a kinematic retargeting method that deforms the MANO model to match robot hand structures and generates dense joint targets while accurately preserving contact relationships.

Established a residual reinforcement learning approach that incorporates object trajectory tracking, finger contact states, and table collision avoidance to stably convert kinematic trajectories into physically feasible demonstrations.

Distilled simulation-generated demonstrations into point-cloud-based visuomotor policies, achieving an 89.3% real-world success rate with zero-shot transfer without any additional learning in the real environment.

sections.heading: How do we grow robot policies from human hand motions?
sections.summary: This section introduces Morphometric Imitation, an end-to-end framework for learning autonomous robot manipulation from human hand-object contact motions. It outlines the design philosophy that seamlessly bridges morphology gaps, preserves contacts, ensures dynamic feasibility, and enables sim-to-real transfer.
sections.details:
Teleoperation is frequently used to collect demonstration data for dexterous manipulation with robot hands. However, teleoperation relies on expensive specialized hardware and requires skilled human operators for many hours, making large-scale data collection difficult. Consequently, approaches that utilize human hand-object interaction (HOI) data from everyday activities have attracted significant interest.

Transferring human motion data to robots typically follows three steps:
- Kinematic retargeting (geometrically mapping human hand poses to robot hand joint angles)
- Dynamic retargeting (refining trajectories in a physics simulator to run stably while accounting for friction and contact forces)
- Policy distillation (learning a visuomotor policy that acts on camera inputs based on the generated trajectories)

However, conventional approaches suffer from major drawbacks. Because human and robot hands differ in size and finger proportions, merely matching fingertip positions disrupts critical contact relationships—where and how the hand touches the object. Furthermore, when natural human desk manipulation is transferred to robots, fingers or the palm frequently collide forcefully with the tabletop.

The core insight of this paper is that explicitly accounting for morphology gaps and contact states from the kinematic retargeting stage dramatically stabilizes both subsequent reinforcement learning and real-world deployment. The authors validate this entire pipeline and demonstrate consistent zero-shot real-world transfer.

sections.heading: Two lineages of retargeting: Kinematics and dynamics
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work in unsupervised kinematic retargeting without wearable sensors and dynamic retargeting using reinforcement learning or optimization. It clearly positions how the proposed approach differs from existing studies and where it makes breakthroughs.
sections.details:
### II-A Trends in Kinematic Retargeting
Conventional retargeting methods often rely on wearable devices like data gloves and motion capture, or manual contact correspondence. Recently, unsupervised methods using 3D hand mesh models estimated from camera images have become mainstream. Representative frameworks such as AnyTeleop and Dex-Retargeting uniformly scale fingertip keypoint vectors based on global hand size ratios. However, they do not account for individual finger proportions or contact surfaces with objects. PyRoki considers fingertip-to-object proximity, and OmniRetarget attempts to preserve contact using tetrahedral meshes, but neither provides a mechanism to fundamentally absorb palm-level structural differences. MMO fundamentally differs by optimizing the human hand model itself to match the target robot's proportions and reconstructing contacts on top of it.

### II-B Dynamic Retargeting and Real-World Deployment
Kinematically transferred joint trajectories often fail when replayed directly in simulation, slipping or bouncing off objects. To resolve this, reinforcement learning (RL) has been widely explored to refine trajectories into physically feasible ones. However, many prior works either constrain human motions in advance so robots can execute them easily, or require real-world teleoperation fine-tuning after simulation. This work distinguishes itself by starting exclusively from unconstrained, natural human motion demonstrations, balancing object trajectory tracking and contact preservation through residual RL, and achieving zero-shot transfer to real hardware.

sections.heading: Mathematics of the base human hand model: MANO
sections.summary: This section explains the structure of MANO, the statistical 3D hand model that forms the foundation of this work. Understanding hand shape parameters, joint rotations, and linear blend skinning provides the basis for the deformation approach in the next section.
sections.details:
The authors adopt MANO, a widely used 3D hand shape model, to geometrically represent human hands. Learned from large-scale hand scan datasets, MANO takes hand shape parameters $\vec{\beta}$ and pose parameters $\vec{\theta}$ (representing joint rotations) as input, and outputs surface mesh vertices $\mathbf{V}$ and 3D joint positions $\mathbf{J}_{\text{posed}}$.

Specifically, it extends Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) to rotate a rest mesh $T_P$ around rest joint positions $J$. MANO has 16 joints including the wrist (15 finger joints + 1 wrist joint). The pose parameters $\vec{\theta}$ consist of global wrist rotation $\vec{\theta}_g$ and local finger rotations $\vec{\theta}_h$. Additionally, pose-dependent corrective offsets (pose blend shapes) are incorporated to prevent skin mesh collapse or unnatural smoothing when joints bend.

sections.heading: How MMO deforms hands to recover lost contacts
sections.summary: This section details MMO, the first stage of the proposed method. It consists of three steps: morphology matching using Scaled MANO that independently rescales the palm and fingers, contact matching to restore disrupted contacts, and robot pose recovery that solves joint angles from dense target poses.
sections.details:
MMO (Morphometric Optimization) is an innovative three-step algorithm designed to bridge the geometric gap between human and robot hands.

### IV-A Morphology Matching
Robot hands often feature thicker fingers or link proportions that differ from human hands. To address this, the authors build "Scaled MANO," an extension of MANO. They introduce a scaling vector $\vec{S} \in \mathbb{R}^6$ to independently adjust the palm scale $S_{\text{palm}}$ and each of the five finger scales $S_i$. To avoid breaking palm vertex blending, the entire hand is first uniformly scaled around the wrist, and then each finger is independently scaled around its metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint. Next, the joint and fingertip positions extracted from the robot URDF are matched against corresponding Scaled MANO points via least-squares optimization (Levenberg-Marquardt), yielding a deformed hand model $M_{\text{morph}}$ that closely matches the target robot's proportions.

### IV-B Contact Matching
Deforming morphology inevitably shifts contact relationships between the human hand and the object. Therefore, the pose of $M_{\text{morph}}$ is re-optimized at each frame to restore the original contacts.
- Contact identification: Vertices on the original human mesh within 5 mm of the object surface are extracted as the contact vertex set $\mathcal{H}_c$. During pre-grasp approach phases where no contact occurs, the model continues referencing vertices from the peak-contact frame to maintain smooth pre-grasp poses.
- Finger coupling: For hands with fewer fingers than humans (such as 3-finger hands), multiple human fingers correspond to a single robot finger; a distance constraint loss $\mathcal{L}_d$ preserves their relative distances.
- Table collision penalty: A penalty $\mathcal{L}_{\text{table}}$ is applied to vertices penetrating below the table plane $z_{\text{table}}$ to prevent desk collisions.
Solving the combined objective yields a hand pose $M_{mc}^t$ that satisfies both morphology and contact constraints.

### IV-C Robot Pose Recovery
The motion of $M_{mc}^t$ is then converted into robot joint angles. Conventional methods often solve inverse kinematics (IK) targeting only 3D fingertip positions, leaving the wrist and intermediate joints in unnatural orientations. In MMO, heat diffusion on 1D skeleton graphs precomputes blending weights between MANO and robot skeletons, generating dense 6-DoF target poses for all robot joints and fingertips. Solving a JAX-accelerated IK with table mesh collision checks recovers collision-free, temporally smooth robot joint trajectories $\mathbf{q}_{\text{ref}}$ in a single pass. This process operates at a fast 180 frames per second on a GPU.

captions.F3: The three-step pipeline of MMO: morphology matching, contact matching, and robot pose recovery. For three hands with completely different kinematic structures (Dex3, Allegro, and Sharpa), morphology-optimized MANO hand models are generated and converted into robot poses while preserving object contact.

sections.heading: Crossing the physics barrier with residual reinforcement learning
sections.summary: This section explains residual reinforcement learning, which refines kinematic reference trajectories into physically executable trajectories inside simulation. By rewarding both object tracking and contact matching, and terminating early on table collisions, it generates safe and stable demonstration motions.
sections.details:
Even when kinematically derived joint trajectories $\mathbf{q}_{\text{ref}}$ are geometrically sound, replaying them in a physics simulator can cause objects to slip away or bounce off due to excessive contact forces. To overcome this, the authors employ residual reinforcement learning (Residual RL) using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) in the ManiSkill simulator. At each step, the policy $\pi$ outputs a small correction $\Delta \mathbf{q}_t$, setting the commanded robot joint angles to $\mathbf{q}_{\text{cmd}} = \mathbf{q}_{\text{ref}} + \Delta \mathbf{q}_t$. Modulating around the reference trajectory dramatically constrains the exploration space.

### Observation and Reward Design
This RL agent trains as a "teacher policy" with access to privileged state information. Observations include proprioception (joint positions), current and future reference joint angles, current and target object poses, and finger contact states (whether contact forces are non-zero).

The reward function is formulated as the product of object tracking and contact preservation:
$r_t = r_{\text{obj},t} \cdot r_{\text{contact},t}$
- Object tracking reward $r_{\text{obj},t}$: Evaluates translational and rotational deviations via an exponential function based on the average point distance (ADD error) of sampled object mesh points.
- Contact reward $r_{\text{contact},t}$: Measures alignment between the target number of contacting fingers $N_{\text{goal},t}$ and the observed contacting fingers $N_{\text{obs},t}$. Normalizing by the robot's total finger count $N_{\max}$ allows fair operation across hands with different numbers of fingers.

### Early Termination and Domain Randomization
Episodes are terminated immediately (Early Termination) upon severe table collisions or excessive contact forces. This rigorously prevents behaviors that could damage real hardware. Furthermore, by randomizing robot PD gains, friction coefficients, object masses, anisotropic scaling, centers of mass, initial placement positions (within a $10\,\text{cm} \times 10\,\text{cm}$ region), and reference start times, the agent produces robust demonstrations. Training completes in 60 to 90 minutes per policy on a single GPU.

captions.F4: Time-lapse sequences of simulation behaviors obtained through residual RL. For the hammer, apple, and cube, stable grasping and manipulation trajectories are generated across 3-finger (Dex3), 4-finger (Allegro), and 5-finger (Sharpa) hands without altering hyperparameters.

sections.heading: Distilling into point-cloud visuomotor policies for real-world deployment
sections.summary: This section covers distilling the privileged simulation teacher policy into a student policy that takes only depth camera point clouds and joint angles as inputs. Using flow matching for diffusion-based policy representation, it enables zero-shot real-world transfer.
sections.details:
Because the residual RL policy trained in simulation relies on privileged information such as ground-truth object meshes and masses, it cannot run directly from real-world camera inputs. Therefore, logs from this teacher policy are collected as a dataset to train a point-cloud-based "student policy (visuomotor policy)" via imitation learning.

### Student Policy Architecture
From point clouds captured by simulated depth cameras, the table surface is segmented out via RANSAC, leaving a clean point cloud containing only the robot and the object. The student policy uses ManiFlow, a recent imitation learning framework.
- Inputs: Current and previous point clouds $(\mathbf{p}_t, \mathbf{p}_{t-1})$, robot joint angles $\mathbf{q}_t$, and previous commanded action $a_{t-1}$.
- Architecture: Combines a point cloud encoder with a DiT-X action generator, outputting joint commands via Flow Matching and Consistency Training.
- Control rate: The policy operates at 10 Hz, predicting joint targets in chunks (sequences of multiple steps) and replanning after executing every 3 actions.

During student training, additional point cloud randomizations simulate depth camera noise, partial dropouts, and residual table fragments. This equips the policy with high robustness against degraded real-world depth observations.

sections.heading: From kinematics to hardware: Exhaustive comparisons and validation
sections.summary: Using three robot hands and ten object manipulation tasks, this section evaluates kinematic contact accuracy, residual RL success rates, ablations, and real-world zero-shot performance. MMO demonstrates clear advantages, highlighted by an 89.3% success rate across 300 real-world trials.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated 10 object manipulation tasks from the GRAB dataset (alarm clock, apple, bowl, cube, cup, flashlight, hammer, light bulb, torus, and wine glass) using three robot hands: 3-finger Dex3, 4-finger Allegro, and 5-finger Sharpa.

### VII-D Kinematic Retargeting Comparison
MMO was benchmarked against five baselines: DexPilot, AnyTeleop, Position, Contact PyRoki, and OmniRetarget. In position-aware contact F1 score (5 mm tolerance), which measures whether contact locations match between hand and object, MMO outperformed the strongest baseline by +8.3 points on Allegro, +27.8 points on Dex3, and +10.5 points on Sharpa across all hands. Contact patch distances were also significantly reduced.

### VII-E Dynamic Retargeting (Residual RL) Evaluation
Using the same residual RL algorithm, task success rates were compared when initialized with reference trajectories from different kinematic retargeting methods. MMO-initialized RL achieved success rates of 82.5% on Dex3, 69.9% on Allegro, and 91.8% on Sharpa, exceeding the strongest baselines (53.2%, 68.2%, and 56.5%, respectively) by up to 35 points. This demonstrates that kinematic contact accuracy directly dictates dynamic simulation success.

Ablating "contact information" from RL rewards and observations significantly dropped success (e.g., from 91.8% to 76.6% on Sharpa), while removing "object pose information" reduced it even further (54.3%). This ablation confirms the complementary relationship where object pose guides task-level trajectory tracking while contact information ensures human-like, stable grasping.

### VII-F Real-World Zero-Shot Transfer (KUKA iiwa14 + Sharpa Hand)
The trained student policies were deployed zero-shot onto a physical KUKA iiwa14 arm equipped with a Sharpa Wave hand. Using an Intel RealSense L515 LiDAR camera, 300 total trials were conducted across 10 categories $\times$ 3 real instances each (30 unique objects with diverse shapes and textures), randomizing initial placements within a $10\,\text{cm} \times 10\,\text{cm}$ region across 10 trials per object.
Overall, the system achieved an 89.3% success rate (268/300 trials). Despite operating on a hard wooden table, there were zero hard collisions. Even for transparent wine glasses where LiDAR beams penetrate, placing a ping-pong ball inside for partial visibility yielded a 93.3% success rate, proving high robustness to point cloud occlusions.

captions.F5: Qualitative comparison of kinematic retargeting on a wine glass (top row: Sharpa) and a bowl (bottom row: Allegro). MMO (Ours) faithfully replicates finger wrapping and shallow thumb placement along the bowl rim, whereas baselines exhibit fingers penetrating the glass or unintended contact points.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: This section summarizes the critical importance of morphology- and contact-aware retargeting as a starting point. It touches on future extensions from per-category policies to multi-task models and direct learning from monocular video demonstrations.
sections.details:
This work presented Morphometric Imitation, an end-to-end framework that derives robot visuomotor policies directly from human demonstration data. By capturing morphology gaps and contacts accurately at the kinematic stage through MMO, refining them dynamically via residual RL, and distilling them through point-cloud imitation learning, it achieves an 89.3% real-world success rate with zero real-world training.

Current limitations and future directions include:
- Policies are currently trained per object category; building unified multi-task policies capable of handling multiple categories simultaneously is a promising next step.
- While this work used high-fidelity motion capture data (GRAB), MMO itself runs fast (180 fps), opening avenues for natural demonstrations reconstructed from monocular RGB video and extensions to bimanual manipulation.

sections.heading: Strict contact evaluation protocols and real-world trial details
sections.summary: This appendix supplements the geometric definitions of contact evaluation, comprehensive baseline comparisons, sensor observation characteristics in physical trials, and success rate variations across initial placement locations.
sections.details:
### Geometric Definition of Contact Metrics
Rather than merely checking if fingertips are near the object, contact metrics compute an area-weighted F1 score measuring whether the robot's corresponding finger contacts the exact surface patch touched by the human finger. Signed distance functions (SDF) rigorously sample object and robot link surfaces, measuring penetration depth into the table and object down to millimeter precision.

### Real-World Sensor Observations and Failure Analysis
The LiDAR depth camera used in physical experiments suffered noticeable dropouts on black or slender objects (such as small black flashlights). However, extensive point cloud dropout and noise randomization during student training allowed the policy to succeed in grasping across most trials despite sparse observations.

Analysis of failed trials revealed two primary failure modes:
- Workspace position sensitivity: Failures clustered along the row closest to the robot base (near row) within the $10\,\text{cm} \times 10\,\text{cm}$ grid (22 of 29 grid failures occurred in the near row). This was likely caused by camera blind spots and arm kinematic limits.
- Unexpected object thickness: Objects thicker than expected, such as a bulky red alarm clock, led to insufficient pre-grasp aperture, pushing the object sideways. Additionally, masking tape used as a torus object had a much thinner cross-section than the training bagel model, yielding the lowest category success rate at 80.0%.

captions.F9: Input point clouds for the real-world policy. Shown are RGB images (for reference), raw depth images, and 512-point segmented clouds (magenta) with the table plane removed. Even for objects with severe point dropouts, such as a black alarm clock or a compact flashlight, the policy correctly perceives and grasps them.

takeaways: In robot hand retargeting, optimizing the morphology of the hand model itself and restoring contact patches—rather than merely matching fingertip positions—governs downstream reinforcement learning success.
For dynamic retargeting, a multiplicative reward combining object trajectory tracking and finger contact matching yields the most stable performance.
Early termination on table collisions during simulation completely prevents violent collisions on hard real-world tables, enabling safe zero-shot deployment.
limitations: Requires training separate reinforcement learning and visuomotor policies for each object category, rather than operating as a single unified multi-task model.
Relies on high-quality motion capture data (GRAB) as input demonstrations; validating performance on noisy 3D reconstructions from monocular RGB video remains future work.
Prone to pre-grasp failures when object geometries deviate substantially beyond the domain randomization range (e.g., extremely thin tape rolls).
